Title: Concern with mild racism of BH vampire art

Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
When Black Hand first came out, there was some discussion on this
newsgroup as to the racist name of "Tarbaby Jack". I can't tell from the
lighting of the card whether the Nosferatu is even black or not.
Probably couldn't tell anyway since he's a Nossie and all. I'm inclined
to think that the term "tarbaby" was probably not meant in the racist
connotation that some people assumed. There are also reasons why the
character might take on such a name. In any case, no real harm done I
think.

But I am a little concerned by the images used for Jesus Alcala, Wah
Chun-Yuen and Blackhorse Tanner.

All three vampires have fantastic art, I must say... no complaints in
that department. I'm just wondering why the artists would choose to use
imagery that is so obviously stereotypical.

Now, I've never been to Mexico, so maybe I'm wrong here, but do Mexicans
actually walk around looking like that? I half expect him to be holding
a taco and riding a burro or something... That said, the image itself is
fantastic IMHO. Coolest image by Steve Prescott yet.

Wah Chun-Yen looks like he is living in Victorian London. A lot of
vampires are anachronisms I guess, but it seems odd to me that the
artist would choose to make an obviously Chinese vampire into some kind
of Charlie Chan, rather than simply making a vampire that happened to be
Chinese. Look at Nicholas Chang. He doesn't seem like a stereotype to
me. He just needs a better haircut maybe.

Along the same lines, Blackhorse Tanner has the whole bead thing going
on. Not too overt, and I've encountered the occasional native here in
Canada that also does the bead thing. No big deal. But it still seems
kind of over-the-top to me somehow. I've met more native Canadians that
don't wear the beads than do. Still, at least Andrew Trabbold didn't
give him warpaint and a full head dress thingy (what the hell are those
called anyway?).

These aren't really meant to be serious complaints so much as
observations. It's not overt racism, nor is it particularly harmful, but
it still seems kind of weird to me. Kind of like saying to a Chinese
person "Oh, you must be good at math."

It seems that White Wolf has been making an effort to include more
minorities in the game (both in the ccg and rpg), which I applaud. Past
mistakes (IMHO) of the Assamites and Ravnos especially are slowly being
addressed by the company, and in as sensitive a way as possible. Not all
"Gypsies" are thieves and not all Arabs/Muslims are terrorist assassins.
Expanding the overall concept of these clans is a good start to
correcting what I view as implicit racism. (Killing off all of the
Ravnos is a little weird, viewed in this light, but I digress :)

I mean it's not like 99% of vampires in the World of Darkness would
really be white heterosexual Euro-types (though I imagine the players
quite likely are).

Including vampires like Chang, Sister Evelyn, Celeste and Banjoko et al
is a good thing I think. Adds some colour to the game... literally. But
I humbly recommend a little bit of sensitivity on the part of the
artists when doing so. If we get a French vampire in Gehenna who is
wearing a beret and carrying a baguette, I'm outta here :)

Anyway, just some thoughts...

Cheers,
WES

P.S. Waaaay back in comic-book history, there was a time when Captain
America was fired by the U.S. government and replaced with another,
slightly more psychotic hero, who took up the same costume and name. The
new Cap was assigned a black side-kick named "Bucky" (after the original
boy wonder who had long since died). Most readers were of course unaware
that "Bucky" had also been used as a racist term for black people.
Obviously, neither had the writers. It was quickly rectified, and in a
very sensitive and innovative way. The writer (the under-rated Marc
Gruenwald) incorporated this into the actual storyline and had "Bucky"
complain about the racist name he was given. Marvel also apologized for
the slip-up. Anyway, I always thought that was a pretty cool way to
address the problem.

P.S.S. For disclosure sake, I am a white heterosexual Euro-type. That's
probably obvious to anyone reading this though :)

misunderstandings in the world about this subject. It is why I want to
see the PC crowd shoved back in the miserable little sewer they came

From www.m-w.com,

Main Entry: rac·ism
1: a belief that race is the primary determinant of human traits and
capacities and that racial differences produce an inherent superiority
of a particular race
2: racial prejudice or discrimination

Jesus Alcala wearing a big honkin' sombrero corresponds to neither of
these definitions, but your incorrect use of the word brings a huge
emotional charge into an issue where it ABSOLUTELY DOES NOT BELONG.

And I am calling "Bullshit" on it.

>Most of the BH expansion, and also all of the past expansions, did not
>strike me as particularly bad in this regard. Francois Villon, as Derek
>mentioned, never struck me as being a stereotype particularly. Nor have many

THIS is the word you are looking for. Again from www.m-w.com,

Main Entry: stereotype
1 : a plate cast from a printing surface
2 : something conforming to a fixed or general pattern; especially : a
standardized mental picture that is held in common by members of a group
and that represents an oversimplified opinion, prejudiced attitude, or
uncritical judgment

Definition #1 is meaningless in this discussion.

Definition #2 would seem, at first glance, to support your misuse of the
word "racism", as one of the three possibilities is that it may
represent a prejudiced attitude. However, reading closer, we also find
the possibility that a stereotype may just be an oversimplified opinion.

Now, which do you think is more likely: that White Wolf has some
irrational grudge against Mexicans, or that the writer and artist have
chosen to deliberately oversimplify their depictions of Jesus Alcala in
order to render a more descriptive picture of the character... or so
that the character may appear as people would expect?

This is why your use of the word "racism" grates so badly on me, and why
I wish to see the whole PC movement thrown in the ditch and kicked until
it stops moving. Careless snap judgements such as this have too much
potential to cause undue controversy (such as this thread), where there
really is nothing to be concerned about.

And what we come back to, after all this rigmarole and shouting, is that
Jesus Alcala is wearing a big dorky hat because the fictional character
he's based on wears a big dorky hat, and THAT is because the job that
said fictional character performs includes a big dorky hat as part of
the costume.

It couldn't make any MORE sense, really.

3rd/Revised Edition of the RPG. They've got plenty of room to play
along a little bit with funny stereotypes than most games. Take a look
at El Diablo Verde in Nights of Prophecy: an obvious joke with the pro
wrestling business, more than just a stereotypical view on Mexicans.

Personally, I won't be offended by any means they'd portrait a
brazilian, as long as I think it's fitting at least to a small portion
of our culture - as the "beret and baguette" thing relates to the old
romantic view of artists in Paris. Every stereotype has its basis, and
as long as nobody abuses that stereotype to the extreme - like an
entire expansion on France using all stereotypes available about the
country - it's normal to see something a little cheesy once in a
while. I'm certain that many brazilians often see americans with a
certain stereotypical point of view, so...

Just to add a curious story: in 2001 we had a big rock festival in Rio
de Janeiro, the 3rd edition of Rock in Rio. The Queens of the Stone
Age were to play at the 'heavy metal' night, and I was there to see
them. When it was their turn to begin the show, the bass player
(forgot his name...) ran up the stage totally naked. Some songs after,
he put his pants on again, and at the end there was some visible
agitation at the backstage. I was hanging around with a group of
friends who happened to be mostly composed of journalists, and they
quickly discovered that the guy was arrested for public nudity.
Later that night we had a chance to see a recorded interview with him
on the press place, and he argued about the arrest using the following
logic: "I've always seen naked girls on brazilian Carnival on TV, so I
thought doing the same was no problem". At first we laughed a lot -
his stereotypical 'dumb' view on Brazilians got him an arrest. Until
we realised the core truth of the matter, the hypocrisy in our own
laws and culture.
First, we enforce appropriate dressing in law but allow all kinds of
exposure on TV films and during Carnival.
Second, all tourist propaganda we got is devoted to promote the most
hedonistic view of the country, but we don't want tourists to get
naked on the beach or on streetcorners while they catch on local
hookers. Sexual tourism began to be confronted seriously by law less
than a decade ago.
Third, the guy is prone to do this every show he does around the
world. Maybe he was well aware of the chance of arresting, but did it
all the same just to see what happens. And in this act he helped us to
think a little bit about our own condition.

The lesson on stereotypes is clear: none of them comes from complete
misunderstanding. This misunderstanding always begins with some
measure of truth. What matters is what you do with the stereotype, and
you can't expect that everyone, always will be able to pass through
that misunderstanding if one had not the chance to get in contact with
the *full* truth (in the bass players' case, actually coming to Brazil
*during* Carnival would do this, per example; he'd see that there's
place and time for public nudity here). The best all we can do is to
enlighten the ignorants, and think about how things lead to the
stereotype. Nothing else is worth the effort, getting upset or
disturbed included.

cheers!
